subject: English
q: Walk carefully lest you ______ slip on the wet floor.
explanation: ‘Lest’ is followed by ‘should’ (or the base form), and it is never followed by ‘not’.

subject: English
q: Keep the medicines on a high shelf ______ the children should reach them.
explanation: ‘Lest’ means ‘for fear that’ and is followed by ‘should’.

subject: English
q: You may borrow my car ______ you return it by evening.
explanation: ‘Provided that’ introduces a condition that must be met.

subject: English
q: Take an umbrella ______ it rains.
explanation: ‘In case’ means ‘as a precaution against the possibility that’.

subject: English
q: You cannot enter the examination hall ______ you have a roll-number slip.
explanation: ‘Unless’ states the only condition under which something will happen.

subject: English
q: Work hard, ______ you will fail.
explanation: ‘Otherwise’ means ‘if not’ and introduces the result of not doing something.

subject: English
q: You can stay with us ______ you keep the house tidy.
explanation: ‘As long as’ means ‘on condition that’.

subject: English
q: No sooner had the bell rung ______ the students rushed out.
explanation: ‘No sooner’ is always followed by ‘than’.

subject: English
q: Hardly had I reached the station ______ the train left.
explanation: ‘Hardly’ is followed by ‘when’ (or ‘before’), not ‘than’.

subject: English
q: Scarcely had the minister begun his speech ______ the lights went out.
explanation: ‘Scarcely’ pairs with ‘when’ (or ‘before’), not with ‘than’.

subject: English
q: No sooner ______ the minister arrive than the protest began.
explanation: After ‘no sooner’, the auxiliary is inverted; with the base form ‘arrive’, the auxiliary must be ‘did’.

subject: English
q: Hardly ______ the match started when it began to rain.
explanation: After ‘hardly’, the past perfect auxiliary ‘had’ is inverted before the subject.

subject: English
q: She is not only intelligent ______ hardworking.
explanation: ‘Not only’ is paired with ‘but also’.

subject: English
q: Not only ______ the examination, but he also won a scholarship.
explanation: When a sentence begins with ‘not only’, the subject and auxiliary are inverted.

subject: English
q: Either you apologise ______ you leave the meeting.
explanation: ‘Either’ is paired with ‘or’.

subject: English
q: Neither the minister ______ his secretary was available for comment.
explanation: ‘Neither’ is paired with ‘nor’.

subject: English
q: Both the teachers ______ the students welcomed the new timetable.
explanation: ‘Both’ is paired with ‘and’.

subject: English
q: We will go ahead with the plan ______ he agrees or not.
explanation: ‘Whether … or not’ presents two alternatives; ‘if’ is not used before ‘or not’ in this position.

subject: English
q: He neither smokes ______ drinks tea.
explanation: The correlative pair is ‘neither … nor’.

subject: English
q: He did not attend the ceremony, ______ did he send an apology.
explanation: After a negative clause, ‘nor’ introduces a further negative and is followed by inversion.

subject: English
q: He was so weak ______ he could hardly stand.
explanation: ‘So’ plus an adjective is followed by ‘that’ to express result.

subject: English
q: It was ______ a hot day that we stayed indoors.
explanation: ‘Such’ is used before a noun phrase (a hot day) in a ‘such … that’ result clause; ‘so’ goes before an adjective alone.

subject: English
q: The lecture was ______ boring that half the audience left.
explanation: ‘So’ is used before an adjective alone in a ‘so … that’ result clause.

subject: English
q: He would rather resign ______ compromise on his principles.
explanation: ‘Would rather’ is followed by ‘than’ when two actions are compared.

subject: English
q: Her performance was as good ______ her sister’s.
explanation: Equal comparison uses ‘as … as’.

subject: English
q: The new policy is not so harsh ______ the critics claim.
explanation: Negative comparison may use ‘not so … as’ (or ‘not as … as’).

subject: English
q: He has no source of income other ______ his pension.
explanation: ‘Other’ in comparison is followed by ‘than’.

subject: English
q: The reason he failed is ______ he did not revise at all.
explanation: After ‘the reason … is’, the clause is introduced by ‘that’; ‘reason … because’ is redundant.

subject: English
q: Please wait here ______ I return.
explanation: ‘Until’ means ‘up to the time when’.

subject: English
q: ______ the rain stopped, we set out for the village.
explanation: ‘As soon as’ means ‘immediately after’.

subject: English
q: ______ I was walking home, it began to rain.
explanation: ‘While’ introduces a clause for an action in progress; ‘during’ needs a noun.

subject: English
q: Always think carefully ______ you speak.
explanation: ‘Before’ introduces the later of two actions.

subject: English
q: ______ the examinations are over, the students can relax.
explanation: ‘Now that’ means ‘because it is now the case that’.

subject: English
q: ______ the forms are submitted, no changes will be allowed.
explanation: ‘Once’ as a conjunction means ‘as soon as’ or ‘after’.

subject: English
q: Do not leave the office ______ the director has signed the file.
explanation: The sense is ‘up to the time that’, so the time conjunction ‘until’ is required.

subject: English
q: ______ the ambulance arrived, the injured man had lost a lot of blood.
explanation: ‘By the time’ introduces a point before which something had already happened.

subject: English
q: He could not attend the wedding ______ he was ill.
explanation: ‘Because’ introduces a reason.

subject: English
q: The flight was delayed ______ dense fog.
explanation: ‘Because of’ is followed by a noun phrase; ‘because’ and ‘since’ need a clause.

subject: English
q: He overslept, ______ he missed the bus.
explanation: ‘So’ introduces a result.

subject: English
q: ______ it was raining heavily, the picnic was cancelled.
explanation: ‘Since’ can introduce a reason, meaning ‘because’.

subject: English
q: He left home early ______ he might reach the office on time.
explanation: ‘So that’ introduces a purpose.

subject: English
q: The meeting was postponed ______ all members might attend.
explanation: ‘In order that’ is followed by a clause; ‘in order to’ and ‘so as to’ need an infinitive.

subject: English
q: He could not have stolen the money, ______ he was in Quetta that day.
explanation: ‘For’ as a coordinating conjunction introduces a reason, meaning ‘because’.

subject: English
q: He behaves ______ he were the owner of the company.
explanation: ‘As if’ introduces an unreal comparison of manner.

subject: English
q: The house is too small for us; ______, the rent is too high.
explanation: ‘Moreover’ adds a further point in the same direction.

subject: English
q: He was unwell; ______, he could not sit the examination.
explanation: ‘Therefore’ introduces a logical result.

subject: English
q: The weather was terrible; ______, the match went ahead.
explanation: ‘Nevertheless’ means ‘in spite of that’ and marks a contrast.

subject: English
q: Exports fell sharply; ______, the trade deficit widened.
explanation: ‘Consequently’ introduces a result.

subject: English
q: The task was difficult, ______ she completed it on time.
explanation: ‘Yet’ introduces something surprising in view of what has been said.

subject: English
q: He is wealthy, ______ he is not happy.
explanation: ‘But’ introduces a contrast.

subject: English
q: Pay the bill by Friday, ______ your electricity will be disconnected.
explanation: ‘Or else’ introduces the consequence of not doing something.

subject: English
q: The minister did not answer the question; ______, he attacked the opposition.
explanation: ‘Instead’ shows that one action replaced another.

subject: English
q: The new bridge is longer ______ the old one.
explanation: A comparative adjective is followed by ‘than’.

subject: English
q: The report criticised the contractors ______ the officials who had approved the design.
explanation: ‘As well as’ means ‘in addition to’.

subject: English
q: Do the exercise exactly ______ your teacher showed you.
explanation: Before a full clause, formal English uses the conjunction ‘as’; ‘like’ is a preposition.

subject: English
q: I doubt ______ the proposal will be accepted.
explanation: ‘Whether’ (or ‘if’) introduces a noun clause of doubt after verbs such as doubt, ask and wonder.

subject: English
q: Between you and ______, I think the plan will fail.
explanation: A preposition such as ‘between’ takes the object case, so ‘me’ is correct.

subject: English
q: People like you and ______ must speak up against injustice.
explanation: ‘Like’ here is a preposition, so it takes the object pronoun ‘me’.

subject: English
q: Everyone except ______ was invited to the reception.
explanation: ‘Except’ is a preposition and takes the object case.

subject: English
q: Nobody but ______ knew the combination of the safe.
explanation: ‘But’ meaning ‘except’ is a preposition, so it takes the object case.

subject: English
q: The principal arranged a special lecture for ______ students.
explanation: After a preposition, ‘us’ is required even when followed by a noun (us students).

subject: English
q: To ______ did you hand over the file?
explanation: After a preposition the object form ‘whom’ is used.

subject: English
q: The officer to ______ the complaint was addressed has been transferred.
explanation: A relative pronoun directly after a preposition must be ‘whom’ for people; ‘that’ cannot follow a preposition.

subject: English
q: The prize was shared by two students, Ayesha and ______.
explanation: The pronoun is in apposition to the object of ‘by’, so it takes the object case.

subject: English
q: My brother and ______ are going to Skardu next week.
explanation: Part of a compound subject takes the subject case.

subject: English
q: The teacher asked Hamid and ______ to stay after class.
explanation: Part of a compound object takes the object case.

subject: English
q: ______ Pakistanis are proud of our cultural heritage.
explanation: In subject position ‘we’ is required, even when followed by a noun.

subject: English
q: It is ______ who am to blame for the delay.
explanation: In formal English the complement of ‘be’ takes the subject case, and ‘am’ agrees with ‘I’.

subject: English
q: My younger brother is taller than ______.
explanation: In formal usage ‘than’ is treated as a conjunction with the verb understood (than I am), so the subject case is used.

subject: English
q: Her daughter is now as tall as ______.
explanation: In formal usage the pronoun after ‘as … as’ is the subject of an understood verb (as she is).

subject: English
q: Let him and ______ handle the arrangements.
explanation: The object of ‘let’ takes the object case.

subject: English
q: Mr Ahmed and ______ will represent the department at the conference.
explanation: A reflexive pronoun cannot replace a subject; the subject form ‘I’ is required.

subject: English
q: If you need any help, please contact my colleague or ______.
explanation: A reflexive pronoun is used only when it refers back to the subject; as an object here, ‘me’ is correct.

subject: English
q: The man ______ I thought was honest turned out to be a fraud.
explanation: ‘I thought’ is parenthetical; the pronoun is the subject of ‘was’, so ‘who’ is correct.

subject: English
q: ______ do you think will win the election?
explanation: ‘Do you think’ is inserted; the pronoun is the subject of ‘will win’, so ‘who’ is used.

subject: English
q: He is the candidate ______ we believe to be the most capable.
explanation: The pronoun is the object of ‘believe’ (we believe him to be), so ‘whom’ is correct.

subject: English
q: She is the social worker ______ we met in Murree last summer.
explanation: The pronoun is the object of ‘met’ and refers to a person, so ‘whom’ is used.

subject: English
q: The boy ______ bicycle was stolen reported it to the police.
explanation: ‘Whose’ is the possessive relative pronoun.

subject: English
q: They live in an old house ______ roof leaks every monsoon.
explanation: ‘Whose’ can be used for things as well as people to show possession.

subject: English
q: The doctor ______ treated my mother has moved to Peshawar.
explanation: ‘Who’ is used for people as the subject of the relative clause.
